planting.note: Divide clumps in late winter before new growth starts and plant into permanently saturated, acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade; site where groundwater seepage or a liner-contained bog bed keeps the root zone wet year-round.

directions: This sedge's core habitat is literally seepage-fed, acid seep swamp forest — the classic Gulf Coast 'baygall' — making it an exceptionally precise match for a shaded, chronically wet toe-of-slope bog bed. Keep the root zone permanently saturated and acidic, mimicking a hillside seep by keeping water moving rather than letting it go stagnant, since it resents drying out even briefly. Division of established clumps in late winter before new growth is the dependable propagation route for home gardeners rather than seed, which germinates slowly and irregularly like most wetland Carex.

planting.note: Divide nursery-propagated stock in spring and plant into calcareous-influenced, constantly moist to wet soil in full shade under hardwood canopy; avoid wild collection given hydrology-driven wild population declines.

directions: A small, neat, shade-tolerant tufted sedge native to Coastal Plain hydric hammocks and bottomland forests from North Carolina to central peninsular Florida, this species is genuinely Gulf-adjacent and distinct from pocosin or bay-bog flora. Its diminutive size under a foot tall makes it a useful woodland-floor fill plant at the base of swamp trees where larger swamp Carex would overwhelm a small bed. Because wild populations are threatened by hydrology changes and forestry disturbance, source only nursery-propagated division stock and keep it in full shade over constantly moist to wet, calcareous-influenced soil.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into a streamside, pond-margin, or rain-garden low spot under light hardwood canopy; give it room and consistent wetness rather than companion-planting it tightly.

directions: A handsome, coarse-textured clumping sedge with dangling seedheads, this species is documented growing under light canopy of red maple and swamp tupelo at Sandhills swamp-forest margins, giving it a direct cypress-tupelo-adjacent pedigree and confirmed Gulf Coast relevance through its Alabama, Florida, Georgia, and Mississippi range. It wants soil moister than typical garden conditions and declines in drier soil or when crowded by neighbors, so give it a streamside or pond-margin low spot with consistent wetness and breathing room. It is one of the few swamp Carex that performs in both partial shade and full sun, offering real placement flexibility.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Carex Trial for the Mid-Atlantic Region

planting.note: Divide or plant plugs in spring at a pond edge, ditch bank, or shaded floodplain-style bed, giving the rhizomatous colony room to spread rather than confining it to a tight border.

directions: A vigorous, rhizome-spreading sedge explicitly recommended as an excellent shade groundcover for wet sites, this species handles shallow standing water and seasonal flooding without complaint, making it well suited to the wet-dry cycling typical of a cypress-tupelo swamp margin recreated in a rain garden. It also serves as a larval host for multiple moth and butterfly species, adding wildlife value to its colonizing habit. Give it room at a pond edge or shaded floodplain-style bed rather than a tight perennial border, and mow or cut back old foliage in late winter to keep colonies tidy.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring and site in a backswamp-style bed that floods seasonally and dries only briefly; it is not drought-tolerant and will decline in freely draining soil.

directions: One of the most robust native beaksedges, this species forms architectural clumps topped with long-beaked seedheads and is documented specifically in alluvial swamp forests, seasonally flooded sloughs, and backswamps — the literal flooded-forest-floor habitat of a cypress-tupelo system. Its height and coarse, beaked seedheads make it a strong vertical accent at the dappled-shade edge of a pond or cypress planting, reading as a structural counterpoint to finer swamp grasses and sedges. It does not spread by rhizome, so it can be used as a specimen clump rather than a groundcover, but it needs a bed that floods seasonally rather than one that simply stays moist.
sources: NC State Common Wetland Plants Guide
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide dense clumps in spring and plant into permanently saturated to seasonally flooded, poorly drained soil in the dappled light of a swamp-forest edge.

directions: A dense, upright clumping rush documented growing in maritime swamp forests, shrub swamps, and shaded wet-woodland clearings with poor drainage, this is a genuine shade-tolerant swamp-forest rush distinct from the many full-sun Juncus already common in cultivation. It tolerates both shaded woodland seepage sites and more exposed disturbed wet ground, giving it flexibility as a transition planting between a shaded bog bed and a sunnier pond margin. Cut back old foliage in late winter before spring growth resumes, and divide clumps as needed to propagate more.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
